q: Describe the relationship between tube width and the rise of water. Use figures.
Narrower tubes give a higher rise. Halving the width doubles the rise (1.0 mm: 30 mm; 0.5 mm: 60 mm), so rise is inversely proportional to width.
Predict the rise of water in a xylem vessel 0.05 mm wide. Show your working.
0.05 mm is 1/5 of 0.25 mm, so the rise is about 5 × 119 = about 600 mm (0.6 m).
A redwood tree is 100 m tall. Use your answer to question 2 to evaluate the idea that capillary action lifts water to the top of trees.
Capillary action alone lifts water only about 0.6 m, far less than 100 m. It helps a little, but most of the lift must come from transpiration pull (cohesion–tension).
Ethanol rises less than water in every tube. Suggest why, using cohesion and adhesion.
Ethanol molecules form fewer hydrogen bonds than water, so they are attracted less to each other (cohesion) and to the glass (adhesion).
Explain why a narrow tube gives a higher rise than a wide one.
In a narrow tube, a larger proportion of the water touches the wall. Adhesion acts around the edge, but the weight depends on the volume, so adhesion can hold up a taller column.
Calculate the mean rate of cooling in water without lard over the first 8 minutes. Give the units.
Explain why the flask cooled faster in water than in air at the same temperature.
Water conducts heat away much faster than air, and its high specific heat capacity lets it absorb a lot of heat while barely warming up.
Describe and explain the effect of the lard.
The wrapped flask fell only 9 °C in 20 min, compared with 19 °C without lard. Fat is a poor conductor of heat, so it insulates, like blubber in seals and whales.
All three curves become less steep with time. Explain why.
The rate of heat loss depends on the temperature difference between the flask and its surroundings. As the flask cools, the difference gets smaller.
Evaluate the flask as a model of a seal in cold water.

Useful for comparing insulation fairly (same size and start temperature). But a seal makes its own heat by respiration, controls blood flow to the skin and has a different shape, so real cooling is slower.
